title: AI, Expert or Peer? Examining the Impact of Perceived Feedback Source on Pre-Service Teachers Feedback Perception and Uptake
extended_summary:
This study examines whether pre-service teachers’ perceptions of feedback and their willingness to act on it depend on the perceived source of the feedback: an LLM, an expert, or a peer. The paper addresses a gap in feedback research by asking not only whether participants can identify the source of feedback, but also how correct or incorrect source recognition shapes cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses to the same feedback message.

The intervention was a randomized experiment in which 273 bachelor’s-level teacher education students at a German university received one of 30 written feedback messages on a mathematics learning goal. The messages were produced by three sources: expert, peer, or ChatGPT-4 (LLM). Participants guessed the source, completed a feedback perception questionnaire, and then revised the learning goal to indicate feedback uptake. Objective feedback quality was coded separately and included in the analyses.

Results showed that source perceptions strongly shaped how feedback was evaluated: LLM feedback was judged more positively when it was misattributed to an expert, supporting an expertise heuristic and indicating a bias in favor of human sources. However, perceived source did not meaningfully predict actual uptake. Instead, feedback quality was the only significant predictor of whether suggestions were implemented. The authors conclude that source-related biases affect how feedback is perceived, but not necessarily how it is used, and argue for stronger feedback and AI literacy in teacher education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with 273 pre-service teachers, but it is not a K-12 student study and the intervention is a single-task feedback manipulation rather than a full classroom implementation. It is methodologically stronger than correlational work, but relevance and ecological generalizability to K-12 direct-comparison settings are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study found meaningful perceptual effects and a modest association between feedback quality and uptake, but no direct behavioral advantage for perceived source and only small-to-moderate descriptive differences across conditions. Overall impact on learning behavior is unclear and not large enough to justify a green/blue rating.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated written feedback on a mathematics learning goal, compared with expert and peer feedback, to examine how source perceptions affect feedback evaluation and uptake.

finding.finding_summary: The task centered on revising a mathematics learning goal about identifying right-angled triangles and the Pythagorean theorem. While feedback source changed perceptions, actual uptake of corrections was driven by feedback quality, not source; LLM feedback had the highest relative uptake (52%) compared with expert (45%) and peer (42%) conditions, but source did not significantly predict implementation in the regression model.
finding.measure: Revision of a mathematics learning goal; correction rate / implemented suggestions; number of mistakes recognized and suggestions implemented
finding.effect_size: R²=.078 for uptake model; ANOVA on suggestions implemented η²=.11; mistakes recognized η²=.37

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined feedback perception, feedback literacy-related judgments, and the ability to recognize whether feedback came from an LLM, expert, or peer. Recognition accuracy was low overall (LLM 36%, expert 41%, peer 46%), and misidentifying LLM feedback as human increased perceived fairness and usefulness, but these perception effects did not translate into uptake.
finding.measure: Feedback perception questionnaire (fairness, usefulness, acceptance, willingness to improve, affect) and source recognition accuracy
finding.effect_size: Fairness interaction b=1.21, p=.042; usefulness interaction b=1.76, p=.009; source recognition ANOVA η²=.031
